legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Forecasting Rare Language Model Behaviors". First author Erik Jones (co-first Meg Tong), with Mu, Mahfoud, Leike, Grosse, Kaplan, Fithian, Perez, Sharma. Affiliations: Anthropic (most authors), Mila (Quebec AI Institute), UC Berkeley. arXiv 2502.16797v1, 24 Feb 2025. No venue is stated, so treat it as a preprint.

COVERAGE: All 25 pages were read, about 85,462 chars, including the appendices. I read the C.2 and E result tables directly. I skimmed the reference list, the extended related work (App. A) and the Gumbel derivation (App. B). pypdf warned about "form XObject invocations" while extracting figure content, so figure axes are garbled. No embedded instructions were found.

CORE CLAIM: A single evaluation output is binary. Each query has a continuous "elicitation probability", the chance one sampled output shows the target behavior. The largest quantiles of that distribution follow a power law in the number of queries (a Gumbel-tail fit). So a small eval set (100 to 1,000 queries) can forecast deployment-scale worst-case risk up to roughly 3 orders of magnitude larger (n up to 90,000 to 500,000). Fit method: OLS on the ten highest elicitation scores, where score ψ = -log(-log p).

HEADLINE NUMBERS (all Gumbel-tail unless noted; baseline is a log-normal fit)
1. Misuse worst-query risk (p.5). Models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new), Claude 3 Haiku and their two base models. Eval size m ∈ {100, 500, 1000}, deployment size n ∈ {10,000 … 90,000}. Metric: mean absolute log10 error. Gumbel-tail 1.7 vs log-normal 2.4. Forecasts land within one order of magnitude 72% of the time. Gumbel-tail underestimates 34% of the time vs 72% for log-normal. An unbiased method would be 50%.
2. Behavior frequency (p.5, Table 3). 19 substances (10 chemical, 9 biological), 1000 random eval sets each, thresholds τ ∈ {0.1 … 0.9}, m ∈ {100 … 1000}. Individual-forecast log error: 0.84 (m=100) to 0.76 (m=1000) vs 3.31 to 4.04 for log-normal. Averaging forecasts over eval sets gives about 0.40 to 0.37 for Gumbel-tail (Table 3b) vs 3.07 to 3.93 for log-normal.
3. Aggregate risk (p.6, Table 4). m=1000, n 10,000 to 500,000, 10 rollouts per setting, forecasting the probability of one specific target output. Mean log error 1.3 vs 2.5 for log-normal. The paper reports 1.286 and 2.523 as table averages. The intro also says "86%" of misuse forecasts are within one order of magnitude, from 900 samples to 90,000. It does not say which of the three metrics that covers, so treat the 86% as unattributed.
4. Misaligned actions (p.8, Sec. 5, App. E). Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) only. Synthetic two-choice questions on power-seeking, self-preservation and self-exfiltration, with 100,000 generated system prompts. Worst-query risk: absolute error 0.05, log error 0.06 vs 0.12 and 0.12 for log-normal. When the eval max was below 0.5: 0.14 and 0.19 vs 0.18 and 0.28. Behavior frequency (eval max below 0.5): log error 1.05 vs 4.10.
5. Red-team compute allocation (p.8-9). Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) vs Claude 3.5 Haiku as query generators. Sonnet costs c ∈ {10x, 20x, 50x, 100x} more; 223 settings. The forecast picks the right model 63% of the time vs 54% for the majority baseline and 50% for chance. It reaches 79% when the true gap exceeds two orders of magnitude.
Also: the correctness extension (p.7) uses Claude 3.5 Haiku with repeated sampling (100 outputs per query, 500 where needed), 10,000 queries. Worst-query absolute error is 0.172 and log error 0.17. It predicts max p > 0.5 correctly 75% of the time.

QUOTES
- p.1 abstract: "the largest observed elicitation probabilities predictably scale with the number of queries."
- p.5: "The average absolute log error is 1.7 for the Gumbel-tail method, compared to 2.4 for the log-normal method."
- p.9 (discussion): "We do not study distribution shifts between evaluation and deployment queries, only shifts in the total number of queries."

LIMITS
- Forecasts are not perfect. They are sensitive to the ten highest points of the specific eval set and to stochastic ground truth. The authors say so on p.2 and p.4.
- Gumbel-tail still underestimates 34% of the time (23.9% on the misaligned-action tasks, Table 7). Both methods are biased. In red-teaming the forecasts overestimate, and the overestimate grows with the forecast length (p.9).
- "Deployment" is simulated. Ground truth is at most 3 orders of magnitude above eval, and queries are resampled from the same pool. Larger scales are asserted, not tested.
- Eval and deployment queries are assumed to come from the same distribution. Adaptive adversaries and distribution shift are not tested.
- Most misuse results use proxies: log-probability of a specific output or keyword, not general correctness. Only a small Claude 3.5 Haiku run checks correctness.
- The misaligned-action tests use synthetic multiple-choice questions on one model. Repeated sampling is costly, and the authors only propose adaptive stopping and importance sampling.
- No uncertainty intervals on the forecasts. The authors do not test whether Gumbel is the right extreme-value family.
- All models are Anthropic's Claude models, and the query generators are also Claude models.

BUILDS ON: Hughes et al. 2024 (Best-of-N jailbreaking, a benchmark-level scaling law); Wu & Hilton 2024 (closest work, single-token behavior forecasting); Brown et al. 2024 and Snell et al. 2024 (inference-time scaling); Perez et al. 2022 (automated red-teaming); extreme value theory (Gumbel).

BEST-FIT NOTE: 09-reading-results.md has these headings: "The error bar on a pass rate", "How many tasks", "Repeats and clustering", and "Pitfalls". The best fit is "Repeats and clustering" (subsection "Repeated trials"). Or use "The error bar on a pass rate" as a "what small evals cannot see" sidebar. The paper is about extrapolating tail risk from a small eval, so it also fits a safety or red-team note, but the listing shows no 10-red-teaming note. The 08-eval notes are 01 to 15: 06-evaluating-agents, 10-evals-in-ci, 11-production-and-the-maturity-ladder, 12-failure-modes and others. None is safety-specific. 11-production-and-the-maturity-ladder or 12-failure-modes are plausible alternatives. I did not open those notes.

FIGURE: Figure 1 (p.1). Log-log plot of the top-quantile risk against n, with the unshaded eval region and the shaded forecast region. It shows the claim at a glance. Figure 3 (p.6) is the accuracy comparison against log-normal, but its text extraction is garbled.
